text.t: Insulin is a tiny protein hormone that tells your body how much sugar is in the blood.
This crystal holds two insulin molecules side by side, each made of an A chain and a B chain.
The A chain is just 21 amino acids long, starting with glycine and ending with asparagine.
The B chain has 30 amino acids.
Cells first make one longer chain, let it fold, then clip out the middle to leave these two pieces.
Three disulfide bridges between cysteines hold this small protein together: one inside the A chain and two joining A to B.
In this crystal, histidine 10 of the B chains grips a zinc ion.
Six insulins gather around two zinc ions to form a hexamer, the form used to store the hormone before release.
This is pig insulin, and it differs from human insulin at only this spot: alanine at the end of the B chain where humans have threonine.

does.t: Insulin is made in the pancreas and released into the blood when sugar levels rise, for example after a meal.
It binds to receptors on liver, muscle and fat cells and tells them to take glucose out of the blood and store it.
As a result, blood glucose falls.

shape.t: Being small lets insulin travel quickly through the blood and be caught easily by receptors on cell surfaces.
Small proteins are hard to keep folded, so insulin is braced by three disulfide bridges.
Carbon-rich amino acids such as leucine and isoleucine cluster in the middle, while charged ones cover the surface facing water.

text.t: Insulin is made by the beta cells of the pancreas and carried in the blood to cells all over the body.

wrong.t: When insulin does not work properly, blood glucose rises dangerously and the result is diabetes mellitus.
Type I diabetes happens when the pancreas fails to make insulin.
It can be treated by replacing the missing insulin, which today is made by engineered bacteria or yeast.

history.who: E.N. Baker, T.L. Blundell, G.G. Dodson, D.M. Hodgkin and colleagues

text.t: This pig insulin structure was worked out from X-ray data reaching 1.5 angstroms.
The study traced how two insulins pair up and how three pairs build a hexamer around two zinc ions.

compare.t: The two insulins in this file span about 4.3 nm from end to end.
A single hemoglobin in this gallery measures about 7 nm, so insulin is one of the smallest proteins here.

text.t: Human insulin has threonine here; pig insulin has alanine.
This histidine holds a zinc ion in the stored form.
This cysteine forms a disulfide bridge with cysteine 7 of the B chain.
